titre: The Anthropocene doesn't exist, at least not officially
accroche: The word has been everywhere for twenty years. In March 2024, the geologists charged with deciding voted against its official adoption.
contenu_vulgarise:
The word “Anthropocene” has been circulating since the early 2000s to designate a new geological epoch, one in which human action would have become the dominant force shaping the planet. It has made its way into newspapers, books, even festival names, to the point that one might think the question was settled. It is not.

## A procedure, a vote

Getting a name into the geological time scale is not a media decision: it is a formal procedure, conducted by the Subcommission on Quaternary Stratigraphy, a body of the International Commission on Stratigraphy, itself attached to the International Union of Geological Sciences (IUGS). The Anthropocene Working Group, active since 2009, had proposed a precise reference site: a core of laminated lake sediments from Crawford Lake, in Ontario, where a spike of radionuclides from nuclear testing would mark, around 1952, the official start of the new epoch.

The ballot opened on February 4, 2024, and closed on March 4. The result: 4 votes in favor, 12 against, 3 abstentions. The Commission's executive committee validated the procedure, and the chairs of the Union's seventeen subcommissions approved it in turn on March 20, 2024, by 15 votes with 1 abstention. The Anthropocene did not become a formal geological epoch.

## Why the refusal

The published objections do not concern the reality of human influence, but the form it was meant to be given. The effects of the human species on climate and landscapes long predate 1952; agriculture, ancient deforestation, and the Industrial Revolution already bear their mark. Fixing a single, global instant, on the model of an asteroid impact, fits poorly with a diachronous phenomenon, whose intensity varies by region and by century. The Union's press release suggests instead treating the Anthropocene as a geological “event,” a category that already exists for major but non-instantaneous phenomena, such as the Great Oxidation Event or the Cambrian explosion.

## What the rejection doesn't change

The official press release itself specifies it: the word will continue to be widely used, by the Earth sciences as well as by the social sciences, policymakers, or the general public. What the vote closes is only its status as an official chronostratigraphic unit, the precise slot that the Holocene, the Pleistocene, or the Jurassic each fill. Officially, we are still in the Holocene, and more precisely in its most recent age, the Meghalayan. The gap between the common use of the word and its real status has since remained almost entirely invisible to the general public.

repere.texte: The vote of the Subcommission on Quaternary Stratigraphy, closed on March 4, 2024, rejected the proposal by 12 votes to 4 (3 abstentions). Crawford Lake (Ontario, Canada) was the candidate site to mark, around 1952, the official start of the Anthropocene.
repere.source: IUGS / ICS, press release of March 20, 2024

carte.punch: The Anthropocene has never been officially adopted as a geological epoch.
carte.idee: The word has been circulating for twenty years, but its adoption as an official geological epoch never happened. In March 2024, the body charged with deciding voted against it, by 12 votes to 4: human influence is judged too old and too diffuse for a single dated marker.

quiz.question: Why did the scientific body charged with deciding reject the Anthropocene as an official geological epoch in 2024?
choix: Because the traces of human influence in the sediments of Crawford Lake turned out to be insufficient
Because the scientific community disputes the reality of human impact on the planet
Because the voting process did not gather enough participants to be valid
Because human influence is judged too old and too diffuse to be marked by a single dated marker
quiz.explication: The rejection is not about the reality of human impact, which is widely recognized, but about the form proposed: fixing a single instant around 1952 fits poorly with a phenomenon that began well before and whose intensity varies by region. The vote did gather a valid quorum, later ratified by the Commission's executive committee.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What was the result of the ballot closed on March 4, 2024?
choix: 4 votes in favor, 12 against, and 3 abstentions
12 votes in favor, 4 against, and 3 abstentions
A majority in favor, later overturned by the executive committee
A tie, for lack of a quorum
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The vote of the Subcommission on Quaternary Stratigraphy, opened on February 4 and closed on March 4, 2024, gave 4 votes in favor, 12 against, and 3 abstentions. The subcommission chairs approved the procedure on March 20.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which site had been proposed to mark the start of the Anthropocene?
choix: A Greenland peat bog, dated to the Industrial Revolution
A sediment core from Crawford Lake, in Ontario
An Australian coral reef marked by bleaching
A fossilized plastic layer on a beach in Bermuda
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The working group proposed the laminated lake sediments of Crawford Lake, in Ontario, where a spike of radionuclides from nuclear testing marked, around 1952, the start of the new epoch.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In which unit of the time scale are we officially?
choix: In the Anthropocene, provisionally adopted in 2024
In the Pleistocene, which was never closed
In the Holocene, and in its most recent age, the Meghalayan
In none, the vote having suspended the official scale
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The rejection leaves the scale unchanged: we remain in the Holocene, and more precisely in the Meghalayan, its most recent age. The word Anthropocene continues to be used, but without official chronostratigraphic status.
